eras: The Belle Époque and the sculpted body
edward
Corset, blouse and long skirt

The corset-supported bust, defined waist and long skirt create a figure very different from today's. High-necked blouses and elaborate sleeves complete the middle-class wardrobe, while walking suits show the growing importance of tailoring. Not every woman wears drawing-room clothes: work, income and rural life call for simpler solutions.
Wool for suits; cotton and linen for underwear and blouses; silk, lace and embroidery for elegant dresses. Petticoats and fastenings are structural elements, not simply decoration.
Wide hats, gloves, ankle boots and parasols. Notice the contrast between the richly detailed bodice and the continuous line of the skirt.
Women's growing participation in sport and public life makes freedom of movement an increasingly visible issue. Elegant dress remains a marker of social class.
A high-necked blouse and midi skirt evoke the period without recreating its corset.
Towards a new freedom
empire
Tunics, raised waists and practical suits

Early in the decade, some couture designs lengthen and simplify the figure through draping and historical references. Restrictive skirts that narrow at the hem also coexist. During the First World War, women's work and material needs favour less cumbersome skirts and separate pieces. Change is neither immediate nor the same everywhere.
Jersey and soft fabrics gain visibility alongside wool and cotton. The practicality of uniforms and service clothing influences the relationship between cut and function.
Ankle boots, smaller hats and practical bags accompany suits. Decoration may be concentrated along a tunic or border.
War changes activities, material availability and social occasions. Luxury clothing and workwear tell parallel stories.
A straight coat over a fluid dress revisits the idea of a long, continuous line.
Waists drop, strides lengthen
flapper
Chemise dress and knitted ensemble

The tubular line reduces emphasis on the waist; belts and seams may sit on the hips. Hemlines rise particularly in the second half of the decade. The beaded evening dress is memorable, but does not represent the entire wardrobe: knitted ensembles and day dresses are equally important.
Knitwear, crêpe and lightweight silks allow movement. In eveningwear, embroidery and fringe can accentuate the rhythm of dancing.
Close-fitting cloche hats, strap shoes and long necklaces. Verticality is the key, rather than the number of sequins.
Leisure, sport and a new urban culture help spread an image of a more mobile woman, with differences across class and generation.
A straight dress with a low belt suggests the 1920s even without fringe.
Fabric follows the body
bias
Bias-cut dress and day suit

The waist returns closer to its natural position and skirts lengthen. Bias cutting places fabric diagonally across its grain, allowing a soft, flowing movement. Cinema glamour makes fluid gowns famous; printed dresses, knitwear and suits remain central to everyday life.
Crêpe, satin and fabrics with good drape are ideal for eveningwear. Manufactured fibres provide alternatives to more expensive silks.
Defined shoulders, small tilted hats and compact bags. Bare backs belong primarily to eveningwear, rather than every occasion.
Economic crisis coexists with the desire for cinematic escapism. Fashion expresses both imagination and concern for the useful life of clothes.
A satin skirt and a simple knit revisit the balance between fluidity and restraint.
Dressing between necessity and renewal
utility
Utility suit and New Look

During wartime, many wardrobes favour structured jackets and relatively restrained skirts. Rationing and regulations differ by country. Mending and reuse become essential skills. In 1947, Dior's New Look offers a change of direction: a narrow waist, shaped bodice and full skirts, attracting both admiration and criticism for their generous use of fabric.
Hard-wearing wool, reclaimed fabrics and substitutes for scarce materials. Post-war dresses may need internal supports and petticoats to maintain their volume.
Sturdy shoes, turbans and functional bags during the war; coordinated accessories in elegant post-war interpretations.
The same decade contains scarcity and the desire to rebuild. It should not be read as a single, unchanging silhouette.
A blazer with defined shoulders or a circle skirt tells the story of two contrasting moments in the 1940s.
Defined waists, many kinds of elegance
full
Circle skirt, sheath dress and twinset

Alongside the full skirt stands the narrow pencil silhouette. The waist often remains a focal point, although experiments also loosen it. Coordinated ensembles embody composed elegance; trousers and casual clothing play a growing role in leisure. Youth fashion introduces new distance from adult conventions.
Printed cottons for summer dresses, wool for suits, taffeta and organza for evening volume. Petticoats may support the fullest skirts.
Court shoes, ballet flats, scarves, small cardigans and handbags. Shoe choices change the character of the same dress.
Couture, ready-made clothing and consumer culture become increasingly interconnected. Italian fashion gains international visibility.
A knotted shirt with a full skirt, or a cardigan over a pencil skirt, offers two interpretations of the period.
Youth, geometry and new horizons
mini
Minidress, A-line silhouette and trousers

Youth fashion challenges the dominance of adult elegance. Miniskirts and minidresses coexist with traditional suits and, towards the end of the decade, hippie influences. Geometric lines and space-age references reshape the relationship between clothing and the body. The spread of trousers further expands wardrobe possibilities.
Jersey, synthetic fabrics, vinyl and experimental materials join wool and cotton. Fabrics with some body help A-line shapes hold their form.
Coloured tights, tall boots, geometric glasses and compact bags. The leg becomes part of the overall design.
Music, youth movements and social change multiply the centres of taste. London is crucial, but not the only centre.
An A-line minidress with opaque tights communicates the period more effectively than a complete costume.
Fashion becomes a chorus of voices
flare
Flared jeans, maxi dress and wrap dress

There is no single uniform: romanticism, workwear, disco and punk coexist. Flared trousers and long skirts lengthen the figure; the wrap dress adjusts its fit through an overlapping fastening. Towards the end of the decade, rips and provocative accessories challenge the rules of elegance.
Denim, knitwear, printed jersey, suede and shiny fabrics for evening. Embroidery and crochet can express a handmade aesthetic.
Platforms, boots, belts and shoulder bags. In punk, safety pins and hardware carry meaning beyond decoration.
Ready-to-wear and musical cultures expand the vocabulary of style. Identities coexist and often contradict one another.
Choose one direction: flared jeans and a shirt, or a maxi dress and cardigan, rather than combining every cliché.
Power, spectacle and experimentation
power
Shoulder-padded suit and sportswear

Broad shoulders and an emphasised waist characterise many interpretations of power dressing. Alongside the business suit, showy eveningwear, aerobics culture and street influences flourish. Japanese avant-garde fashion proposes volumes and asymmetry that challenge the sculpted body dominant in other settings.
Tailoring wool, leather, stretch jersey, shiny fabrics and technical materials. Internal structures and shoulder pads radically change the proportions of the torso.
Large earrings, statement belts, court shoes or trainers, depending on the context. A single accessory can become the focus of the silhouette.
Television, music videos and the visibility of women in professional life make image a powerful means of communication.
A structured blazer over simple pieces retains the energy without requiring a full suit of shoulder-pad armour.
Minimalism and everyday rebellion
slip
Slip dress, denim and checked shirt

Minimalism reduces ornament and makes cut and drape important. The slip dress brings a form close to underwear into evening dressing. In parallel, grunge combines seemingly uncoordinated garments, knits and boots. Streetwear and hip-hop culture help redefine volume, branding and belonging.
Satin, jersey, denim, flannel and leather. Simple fabric can become refined through its cut; worn surfaces may be deliberately sought as a style statement.
Minimal sandals, combat boots, trainers and compact bags. Changing shoes transforms the slip dress from delicate to urban.
Luxury fashion and subcultures observe each other and borrow one another's forms and symbols.
A fluid dress with a T-shirt, or straight jeans with a clean-lined knit, recalls two different sides of the decade.
The Y2K imagination
y2k
Low-rise trousers, cargo pants and crop tops

Low waistlines alter the proportions between torso and legs; crop tops, decorated denim and cargo trousers gain visibility. Pop culture amplifies metallic details and recognisable accessories. Boho, romantic dresses and more conventional office clothing also coexist: the decade is not limited to celebrity looks.
Stretch denim, jersey, sporty velour, metallic finishes and layered lightweight fabrics.
Small shoulder bags, decorative belts, glasses and substantial soles. The relationship between waistband and top hem is decisive.
The internet and celebrity photography accelerate the circulation of looks. Branding may become a visible part of the outfit.
Comfortable cargo trousers with a simple top reference Y2K without making an extremely low waist compulsory.
The connected wardrobe
sport
Athleisure, trainers and oversized silhouettes

Sportswear becomes firmly established in everyday settings. Leggings, trainers and sweatshirts coexist with minimalism, romantic dresses and tailoring. Oversized silhouettes redraw the relationship with the body, while digital images and platforms make styles from different cities visible at the same time.
Technical knits, denim, sweatshirt cotton and tailoring fabrics often appear in the same look. Comfort and performance become fashion talking points.
Trainers, backpacks and cross-body bags; highly recognisable accessories may coexist with neutral basics.
The communication of style increasingly passes through creators, communities and digital commerce. The speed of images does not match the lifespan of clothes.
A tailored jacket with trainers neatly expresses the meeting of formal and informal codes.
Many aesthetics in one wardrobe
modern
Comfort, revival and personal style

This period remains open: the pandemic, a return to social life and the digital circulation of revivals have prompted different responses. Comfortable pieces, relaxed tailoring, Y2K references and occasionwear coexist. Resale and repair offer tools for building a personal wardrobe, without automatically making every second-hand purchase sustainable.
Cottons, knits, technical fabrics and reclaimed materials. Assessing a garment means reading its composition, construction, care requirements and expected lifespan.
Trainers, ballet flats, large or small bags: there is no single compulsory accessory. The choice depends on actual use.
It is more useful to observe practices and communities than to declare a single worldwide trend. A runway does not capture an entire society.
Start with the pieces you actually wear: a new proportion or combination can change a wardrobe more than ten purchases.
regions: occidente
Western Europe and North America
utility
Couture, ready-made clothing and urban dress

Paris, London, Milan and New York are important centres, but represent specific networks rather than all Western women. Between 1900 and 1930, the shift from a constructed bodice to looser lines changes the urban silhouette. War, work and sport make separate pieces more central.

From the 1940s to the 1960s, rationing, post-war couture and youth clothing coexist. From the 1970s, trousers, denim and ready-to-wear expand the combinations. In the 1980s the suit expresses authority, while streetwear and minimalism multiply the alternatives.
From the 1990s to today, the boundary between formal and everyday clothing becomes more porous. Differences between a financial centre, a small town and a rural community remain essential.
Suit: a jacket with a skirt or trousers; trench coat: a belted overcoat with details of military origin; sheath dress: a relatively close-fitting, straight-lined dress.
Do not confuse advertising images with how often garments were actually worn. To understand an outfit, ask where, by whom and for what occasion it was used.

italia
Italy: tailoring and everyday life
full
From dressmaking to Made in Italy

At the start of the century, elegant wardrobes engage with French models; local dressmakers and domestic sewing adapt cuts and fabrics to practical means. The blouse and skirt and the walking suit coexist with work clothes showing considerable regional variety.

After the war, Italian fashion gains international exposure alongside a production system encompassing tailoring, textiles and accessories. Between the 1960s and 1980s, ready-to-wear acquires a decisive role: clothing is also conceived as a serial product that can be coordinated.
Denim, knitwear, coats and occasion dresses describe a varied present. Italian style encompasses work, ceremony, leisure and experimentation, rather than a single model of elegance.
Wool suit; cocktail dress; coordinated knitwear; tailored coat. Quality also depends on linings, seams, fit and the possibility of repair.
Notice how a jacket shapes the shoulder and how a skirt falls when someone walks: fashion can also be understood through movement.

est
Eastern Europe and the former Soviet region
power
Modernity, availability and textile memory

The histories of Poland, Romania, Ukraine, Russia and the Balkans are not interchangeable. In the early twentieth century, international urban clothing and regional dress coexist. Embroidery and weaving may express precise local affiliations.

In socialist countries, ideals of practicality interact with fashion houses, tailoring, industrial production and unequal access to goods. Women alter and sew clothing while continuing to seek elegance, colour and individuality. Conditions vary by country and period.

From the 1990s, markets and trading networks change. Contemporary designers reinterpret local elements alongside the global language of tailoring and streetwear. War and migration affect production and the preservation of heritage.
Shirtdresses, suits, knits and coats; embroidered shirts such as the Ukrainian vyshyvanka belong to specific histories and have many variations.
Embroidery is more than a generic decorative motif. Check the community, technique and context before assigning it a meaning.

giappone
Japan
kimono
Kimono, Western clothing and the avant-garde

In the early twentieth century the kimono remains central for many women as Western forms spread. Kimono construction creates volume through relatively flat surfaces, wrapping and the obi: a different logic from the shaped Western dress.

After the war, Western everyday wardrobes grow. The kimono retains ceremonial and creative roles. From the 1970s and 1980s, Japanese designers contribute to international fashion through experiments with volume, asymmetry, fabric and distance from the body.
Tokyo has many street-style scenes: not all Japanese fashion is kawaii or Harajuku. Today Western clothing, vintage, experimental design and reinterpreted kimono can coexist.
Kimono: a wrapped garment adjusted with the obi; yukata: a generally informal variation, often in cotton; hakama: a pleated lower garment worn in specific contexts.
Look at sleeve shape, length, motif placement and the formality of the fabric. Do not automatically assign identical meanings to every kimono.

cina
China and Hong Kong
qipao
The qipao and Chinese modernities

The twentieth-century qipao changes over time: early urban versions do not all have the narrow line most recognisable today. Shanghai becomes an important laboratory of modernity, bringing local tailoring into contact with international techniques.

More shaped interpretations emerge during the 1930s and 1940s. Political developments in mainland China and Hong Kong's fashion networks then lead to different paths. Utilitarian clothing does not erase every practice of personal distinction.

Today, occasionwear qipao, international fashion and reinterpretations of historical dress are different phenomena. Hanfu and qipao are not synonyms; their historical references and construction differ.
Qipao or cheongsam: a dress with numerous variations in length, fit, sleeve and fastening. A high collar and side slits alone cannot date an example.
Look at fastening position, seams and the proportions of the slit. The famous cinematic version does not summarise a century of Chinese clothing.

corea
Korea
hanbok
Hanbok and the contemporary wardrobe

Women's hanbok commonly includes the jeogori, a jacket, and chima, a skirt. Proportions, materials and ways of wearing them change over time: there is no eternally identical form. In the early decades of the twentieth century, reform, local clothing and outside influences interact.

After the division of the peninsula, political and production paths diverge. In South Korea Western clothing becomes more widespread in everyday life; hanbok retains festive, family and ceremonial roles.

Designers and craftspeople also propose modern hanbok. Seoul fashion, historical drama costumes and K-pop looks are connected but distinct fields. Stage costumes do not describe how an entire population dresses.
Jeogori: the upper garment; chima: the skirt; ribbons and layers contribute to the composition. Material and colour need to be read in context.
Distinguish historical reconstruction, present-day ceremonial clothing and everyday adaptation. A sleeve or skirt may borrow a reference without reproducing it completely.

india
South Asia
sari
Sari, salwar kameez and regional diversity

India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and neighbouring countries encompass different traditions and communities. A sari is draped fabric: its form depends on both weaving and the way it is worn. It does not correspond to a single, uniform national costume.

During the twentieth century, urbanisation, cinema, textile industries and political change reshape tastes and availability. Sari, salwar kameez and other ensembles coexist with Western clothing according to place, occasion and preference.
Today, richly worked bridal clothing and professional wardrobes tell of different needs. Handwoven textiles and new tailoring constructions interact with industrial production.
Sari: a draped length of fabric; salwar kameez: trousers and tunic, often with a dupatta; lehenga: a skirt in an ensemble that may include a blouse and veil.
Cotton, silk and weaving technique change weight and drape. Not every shiny fabric is silk, and not every motif is printed.

filippine
The Philippines and Southeast Asia
terno
The terno and its butterfly sleeves

In the Philippines, baro't saya comprises a blouse and skirt. The ensemble evolves during the early twentieth century; sleeves become one of its most recognisable elements. Family photographs help reveal differences between ceremony, social class and everyday life.

The modern terno develops into a recognisable coordinated or unified dress with butterfly sleeves. After the war, these sleeves retain a strong symbolic role. It is not, however, the universal everyday clothing of Filipina women.

Today the terno is reinterpreted for events and formal occasions. Elsewhere in Southeast Asia, kebaya, áo dài and batik clothing belong to distinct traditions: placing them side by side invites comparison, rather than treating them as equivalent.
Terno: a stiff, arched sleeve structure; baro't saya: blouse and skirt; piña: cloth made from pineapple fibres, used in specific contexts within Philippine tradition.
Notice how the sleeve rises from the shoulder: it is a constructed shape, not simply a puffed sleeve.
https://folklife.si.edu/magazine/filipina-terno-history
medio-oriente
The Middle East and North Africa
kaftan
Long garments, tailoring and personal choices

The area encompasses very different religious, political and climatic histories. In the early twentieth century, local garments, urban dress and European influences coexist. It is inaccurate to imagine a single way of dressing from the Atlantic coast to the Gulf.

Professional clothing, tailoring and public occasions change throughout the century. Moroccan caftans, Gulf abayas and urban suits are not the same thing. Changes in social and political norms affect individual choices in different ways.

Contemporary fashion encompasses luxury design, everyday clothing and modest fashion, which also crosses other countries and religions. Coverage, decoration and structure can all be sites of experimentation.
Caftan: a long garment with regional variations; abaya: a long outer garment in many Gulf contexts; hijab: a term whose uses and meanings need context, not a synonym for an entire outfit.
Do not infer personal beliefs from a garment. To study construction, look at openings, layers, fabrics and movement.
https://www.vam.ac.uk/exhibitions/africa-fashion
africa
Sub-Saharan Africa
wrap
Textiles, identity and contemporary design

A continent does not have a single wardrobe. In the twentieth century, local weaving, commercial exchanges, colonialism and missions interact with specific tailoring practices. Wrapped textiles and sewn garments coexist in many communities.

Independence movements and new cultural networks give clothing further political meaning. Tailors, designers and customers transform available materials, including imports, into local visual languages. Wax prints have a transnational history, rather than a single African origin.

Lagos, Dakar, Johannesburg and other cities have their own design scenes. Material research, photography, craftsmanship and streetwear contribute to global fashion. Tradition is not a stage superseded by modernity.
Àdìrẹ: resist-dyed textiles in the Yoruba tradition; kente: strip-woven cloth with specific origins and contexts; boubou: a loose garment found in several variations.
Name the technique and provenance when you know them. A generic “African” motif erases important differences.

sudamerica
South America and the Andean world
pollera
Pollera, weaving and contemporary cities

European-influenced urban clothing coexists with Indigenous and Afro-descendant practices. In the Andes, layered skirts, shawls and headwear take on local meanings connected to communities, trade and colonial history. The pollera is not identical in every country.

During the twentieth century, migration to cities and changes in work alter occasions and materials. Women may retain, adapt or abandon regional elements. Choices do not follow a single path towards Western clothing.

Contemporary fashion also values cholita identity and textile work alongside streetwear and urban design. In Brazil, beachwear is an important sector, but does not represent the country's entire fashion scene.
Pollera: an often full skirt with different regional constructions; lliclla: an Andean cloth or shawl; camelid-fibre textiles: materials that need precise identification.
Distinguish everyday dress, festive clothing and performance costume. A festival photograph does not automatically describe an everyday wardrobe.

centroamerica
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean
huipil
Huipil, embroidery and community histories

Indigenous communities in Mexico and Central America preserve and transform weaving and embroidery knowledge. A huipil is a blouse or tunic made from panels: dimensions, design and materials vary greatly according to place and use.

During the twentieth century, industrial cotton, new yarns and sewing machines circulate alongside handwork. Technical changes do not erase a garment's cultural value. African, European and local legacies intersect in the Caribbean.

Designers, cooperatives and craftswomen work between continuity and innovation. The commercial use of motifs raises questions of attribution and compensation: recognising the maker is part of understanding the garment.
Huipil: a panelled garment, often embroidered or woven with designs; rebozo: a Mexican shawl with many variations; Panamanian pollera: an outfit distinct from the Andean skirts of the same name.
Do not call every embroidered blouse “Frida”. Look instead for the community's name, technique, material and documented provenance.
https://statemuseum.arizona.edu/online-exhibit/what-would-frida-wear/mexican-textiles
oceania
Oceania and the Pacific
wrap
Climate, colonialism and island creativity

Australia and New Zealand interact with European fashion networks, while Pacific cultures have their own textile and ornament traditions. Clothing introduced by missions intersects with local forms, often through creative transformation.

During the twentieth century, daywear, beachwear and sports clothing coexist with ceremonial garments and community practices. Indigenous peoples' histories are not identical to those of dominant colonial societies.
Māori, Pacific Island and Australian First Nations designers redefine the relationship between identity and contemporary fashion. A cultural motif requires context and attribution.
Wrapped cloths, loose dresses and tailored garments are families of forms, not interchangeable names. Tapa and weaving techniques have specific uses that need to be checked for each community.
Do not reduce the Pacific to a holiday aesthetic: textiles and clothes can tell stories of social relationships, ceremonies and belonging.

glossary: Silhouette
The overall outline created by clothing: column, A-line, hourglass or a shape with displaced volume.
Bias cut
Cut diagonally to the warp and weft, helping a fabric fall more fluidly.
Natural waist
The anatomical waistline, as distinct from a raised or dropped waist.
Dropped waist
A seam or belt placed below the natural waist, often towards the hips.
Circle skirt
A very full skirt made with a circular or related construction.
Pencil skirt
A relatively narrow skirt that follows the hips and may need a slit for walking.
A-line
A shape that is narrower at the top and progressively wider towards the hem.
Pleating
Regular folds that create volume and movement; their permanence depends on material and treatment.
Draping
The arrangement of fabric through flowing folds, gathers and wrapping.
Jersey
A knitted fabric, often soft and stretchy because of its construction; not the name of a fibre.
Satin
A weave with a smooth, shiny surface; it may be made from silk or other fibres.
Crêpe
A family of fabrics with a more or less grainy surface.
Taffeta
A compact fabric with some stiffness, suited to clearly defined volume.
Organza
A light, transparent fabric with good body, often used for layers.
Tweed
A usually woollen fabric with characteristic surface and colour effects.
Denim
A twill fabric associated with jeans: not all denim has the same weight or stretch.
Haute couture
A regulated category of French high fashion, rather than a generic synonym for expensive clothing.
Ready-to-wear
Clothing offered in standard sizes, as distinct from made-to-measure garments.
Bespoke and made-to-measure
Garments constructed or adapted for a customer; the degree of customisation needs to be checked.
Wrap dress
A dress with overlapping sections and an adjustable fastening.
Slip dress
A fluid dress referencing the petticoat or slip, often with narrow straps.
Shirtdress
A dress borrowing elements from a shirt, such as a collar and button fastening.
Peplum
A frill or small added volume at the waist or hips.
Colour blocking
The combination of clearly separated areas of colour.
Upcycling
Transforming existing materials or garments into a new object; the actual impact needs to be assessed.
Vintage
A garment from an earlier period: authentication requires labels, construction and provenance.
Revival
The return of past forms in new clothing; not the same as an original period piece.
Modest fashion
Clothing oriented towards covering the body, with different motivations and interpretations.
